description: Full documentation for remote-store: tutorials, how-to guides, API reference, and design explanations. Write file storage code once, run it against local files, S3, SFTP, or Azure.
rules: Docs follow the Diataxis framework: tutorials for learning by doing, guides for task-focused how-tos, reference for API detail, explanation for the reasoning behind design choices.
The hands-on intro to remote-store. By the end you'll have a working Store reading and writing files across multiple backends by changing only config — and the rest of the docs will make sense.
Guides solve real tasks end-to-end: pick a backend, wire in caching or retry, stream large files, integrate with PyArrow or Dagster. No background reading required — one page, one task.
The reference is exact and searchable — come here when you know the name of what you need or want to dig into type signatures, capability flags, and WriteResult fields.
Why remote-store is shaped the way it is — the reasoning behind design choices, not just what they are. Read when 'how' isn't enough.

Build Your Own Backend — if your storage target isn't a built-in backend, this guide walks you through the full Backend contract: declare capabilities, implement CRUD, map exceptions, and get automatic Store scoping and extension support.

Data Lake Patterns — remote-store as the swappable I/O layer under Delta Lake, Iceberg, or Parquet. Develop locally against MemoryBackend, deploy to S3 or Azure by changing config alone. child() scopes Bronze/Silver/Gold without separate credentials.

Parquet Datasets — ext.parquet.ParquetDatasetStore adds manifests, _SUCCESS completion markers, and part-file layouts so consumers never read a partially-written dataset. Row counts, schema hashes, and custom metadata travel with the data.
Extensions add composable higher-level operations — batching, TTL caching, integrity checking, progress hooks, cross-store transfer — without changing your backend or breaking existing Store calls.
RetryPolicy gives unified retry configuration across all backends; each backend maps it to its native mechanism so retries never multiply when middleware and the backend both retry independently.
